newsitem.title: ITALY: Bossi's rebel "republic" scorned in Italy.
newsitem.headline: Bossi's rebel "republic" scorned in Italy.

text.p: Separatist firebrand Umberto Bossi faced a mixture of scorn and anger after proclaiming a rebel republic in affluent northern Italy.

Ignoring the constitution and popular opposition, he baptised his would-be "federal republic of Padania" at a rally in the lagoon city of Venice and announced the formation of a five-member "provisional government".

"Woe betide the centralist system if it dares touch a single member of the government of Padania. All for one and one for all!" he told a flag-waving crowd of Northern League party supporters numbered by police at fewer than 20,000 people.

Sunday's rally was meant as the climax to a three-day "March to the Sea" by Bossi from the source of the River Po which he had confidently predicted would draw more than one million followers of his drive to split Italy.

His chorus of critics declared the trek a massive flop after media estimates of the League's total turnout along the 625 km (405 mile) river were a maximum 150,000 -- no more than the number police said had flocked to Milan on Sunday for just one of several pro-unity rallies across Italy.
"Bossi had spoken of millions of people who would turn out but frankly no one saw them, not even Bossi," said deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni.
Responding to threats by Bossi to form his own militia, he said the centre-left government "will not tolerate any campaign to recruit any national guard, which I imagine would be armed".

Bossi, who aims to extend his would-be "state" as far south as the central region of Umbria, paved the way for his symbol-laden weekend pilgrimage with a rash of inflammatory statements that had hogged newspaper headlines for weeks.

But while his failure to draw big crowds brought a sigh of relief across the mainstream political spectrum, government and opposition acknowledged that the northern discontent he has seized on to draw support had to be tackled fast.

All parties now agree that radical federal reform -- Bossi's previous agenda -- must be pursued to answer popular frustration with high taxes and stifling central government bureaucracy in the powerhouse northern heartlands of Italy's economy.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi urged Bossi to "come to his senses" and join the search for reform while preserving unity.
"We must re-establish dialogue. I'm ready to talk as of tomorrow (Monday) and to understand and make myself understood about what needs to be done for the country," he told reporters.
Hard-right leader Gianfranco Fini, whose National Alliance party organised the Milan march, said Bossi had staged a "colossal bluff" and should be treated as a political "nobody".
But he added: "All of us, in political terms, have got to provide answers to the real issues of the north".
The League won 10.6 percent of votes at last April's general election to become the fourth biggest party in Italy.
Attendance at Bossi's weekend of rallies appeared to confirm that his switch to a secessionist campaign since the election had undercut his support, even among League voters.

His declaration of "independence" defied a constitutional ban on any challenge to the unity of the state and prompted a call from a former constitutional court president, Ettore Gallo, for his immediate arrest.

But one of Bossi's most prominent critics from the League, former parliamentary speaker Irene Pivetti, said criminal investigations, already under way by magistrates in Turin, would only play into his hands.
"It is political suicide because they're giving him the aura of a martyr and that it just what he wants," said Pivetti, summarily expelled from the League last week for opposing Bossi.
